name: CSEP / ETAS next-day earthquake forecast testing. Core: Lombardi & Marzocchi (2010a), 'The ETAS model for daily forecasting of Italian seismicity in the CSEP experiment' (Annals of Geophysics 53(3):155-164). Companion: Lombardi & Marzocchi (2010b), 'The Assumption of Poisson Seismic-Rate Variability in CSEP/RELM Experiments' (BSSA 100(5A):2293-2300). Follow-ups: Taroni et al. (2018), prospective CSEP-Italy evaluation (SRL 89(4):1251-1261), and Brehmer, Kraus, Gneiting, Herrmann & Marzocchi (2024), 'Enhancing the statistical evaluation of earthquake forecasts - an application to Italy' (SRL, arXiv:2405.10712)
type: method family (paper cluster: ETAS point-process forecaster plus the CSEP prospective-testing protocol and its critiques)
url: https://doi.org/10.4401/ag-4848 (PDF: https://www.annalsofgeophysics.eu/index.php/annals/article/view/4848/4915 ; repository: https://www.earth-prints.org/handle/2122/6419) ; companion BSSA: https://doi.org/10.1785/0120100012 (https://www.earth-prints.org/handle/2122/6420) ; Taroni et al. 2018: https://doi.org/10.1785/0220180031 ; Brehmer et al. 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10712 (https://doi.org/10.1785/0220240209) ; Werner et al. 2010 CSEP-Italy retrospective (shows the Poisson count intervals are too narrow): https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.1092
year: 2010 (both Lombardi & Marzocchi papers); follow-ups 2018 (prospective 5-year results) and 2024 (re-evaluation with proper scoring rules and the Diebold-Mariano test)
authors: Anna Maria Lombardi, Warner Marzocchi (INGV Rome). Follow-ups: M. Taroni, W. Marzocchi, D. Schorlemmer, M.J. Werner, S. Wiemer, J.D. Zechar, L. Heiniger, F. Euchner (2018); J.R. Brehmer, K. Kraus, T. Gneiting, M. Herrmann, W. Marzocchi (2024)
popularity: Crossref citations (retrieved 2026-10-17): Annals paper 19, BSSA Poisson paper 28. Semantic Scholar: Taroni et al. 2018 has 70 citations, Brehmer et al. 2024 has 5. The CSEP protocol itself is the standard testbed in statistical seismology.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (Annals of Geophysics; BSSA; SRL). Brehmer et al. is peer-reviewed in SRL, with an arXiv post-print.
target_type: Count/onset target (a new event occurs), not a state target. CSEP daily forecasts give the expected number of new M>=4 earthquakes, or P(at least one event), in each 0.1 x 0.1 degree cell for the next day. There is no 'state' analogue, because an earthquake has no duration. The closest match to our task is P(at least one new onset in (t, t+H]) per unit.
target_definition: Daily probability of at least one earthquake with ML >= 4.0 in each 0.1 x 0.1 degree cell of the CSEP-Italy testing region, at depth < 30 km. H = 1 day. Forecasts are issued every day using all seismicity up to the start of the window. The ETAS model is fitted on ML >= 2.5 events and rescaled to ML >= 4.0 with Gutenberg-Richter (b = 1.0). The Brehmer et al. 2024 re-evaluation used 7-day expected counts, issued daily, over 8,993 cells.
spatial_unit: grid cell (0.1 x 0.1 degree, CSEP-Italy testing region); also evaluated region-wide (number test) and over the spatial distribution (reliability / S-test)
at_risk_masking: Not applicable in the usual sense. Earthquakes are instantaneous, so no 'already under event' state needs masking. The analogous hygiene is about the conditioning history: forecasts condition only on events before the window start, and ETAS explicitly simulates the events expected during the window (secondary triggering) instead of reading them from the catalogue.
data_sources: INGV Italian seismic bulletin (Bollettino Sismico Italiano). Learning set: 16 Apr 2005 to 1 Jun 2009, 2,100 events with ML >= 2.5 and depth < 30 km. Testing set: 1 Jun 2009 to 1 Sep 2009, 179 events (retrospective, out-of-sample in time). Prospective CSEP-Italy experiment from 1 Aug 2009. Over 5 years Taroni et al. 2018 counted 83 target events with 3.95 <= M < 4.95 and 14 larger shocks.
data_source_variant: Single official catalogue (INGV). The start date 16 Apr 2005 was chosen deliberately: the network and the data processing changed then, so earlier data were not mixed in. This is the analogue of our 'never mix the official file with alerts.in.ua' rule (D-007/D-015) and of starting the series at a regime boundary.
preprocessing: Magnitude-of-completeness analysis (Cao and Gao b-value stability, ZMAP). Mc = 2.0 overall, but Mc rises to about 2.5 right after the L'Aquila Mw 6.3 mainshock and varies in space; Mc = 2.5 chosen as reliable for most of Italy. Depth < 30 km filter. Events restricted to the CSEP collection polygon. No declustering: clustering is modelled, not removed.
known_label_artefacts: (1) Incompleteness after large events: detection drops right after a mainshock, so small aftershocks are missing. The authors list this as a known weakness and suggest a modified magnitude distribution. This mirrors our recording gap (2026-08-30 to 09-01), which must be treated as missing, not as zero (D-013). (2) Spatial heterogeneity of completeness: Mc is higher in southern Apulia and western Sicily, and the authors accepted this as a known limitation. (3) Network change in April 2005: handled by cutting the series at that date. (4) Regime failure: the Italy-wide ETAS fit did not reproduce the early L'Aquila sequence. The local alpha (1.5 to 2.0) exceeds the national 1.3, and the Runs test on learning residuals rejected independence (p = 0.007) until the L'Aquila sequence was removed (p = 0.07). The analogue for us is that a pooled model can misfit one oblast during an unusual campaign. Duplicates and swapped columns were not discussed.
model_family: Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model: a self-exciting (Hawkes) space-time-magnitude point process. Conditional intensity = background rate nu*u(x,y) + the sum over past events of K*exp(alpha*(Mi - Mc)) * (t - ti + c)^(-p) * spatial kernel (d, q) * the Gutenberg-Richter magnitude density. Fitted by maximum likelihood with the Zhuang et al. 2002 iterative stochastic-declustering algorithm. Forecasts are the average over 1,000 simulated catalogues per window (Ogata thinning), so the triggering during the window is included.
features: No engineered features. The model uses only the past event history (times, locations, magnitudes). Fitted parameters: nu = 237 +/- 8 per year; K = 0.011 +/- 0.001; p = 1.16 +/- 0.02; c = 4e-5 years; alpha = 1.3 +/- 0.1; d = 1.10 +/- 0.05 km; q fixed at 1.5 because of the q-d trade-off; log-likelihood -7808.1. 46% of events were classed as triggered, 54% as background. The background spatial density u(x,y) comes from a Gaussian kernel with variable bandwidth. The Omori decay implies P(an M3 event triggers an M2.5+ event) < 1% after 5-6 hours, against 2-3 days for M5 and about 1 month for M7. The analogues for us are 'minutes_since_last_start', 'onsets_last_24h/7d' and 'neighbors_active', which are crude, non-parametric stand-ins for the triggering kernel.
external_feature_timing: None. The model is purely endogenous (catalogue only), with no tectonic, geodetic or geological inputs. All conditioning history ends at the start of the forecast window, which is causal by construction.
ablation_design: No feature ablation. Later CSEP-Italy comparisons ranked whole models (LM = this ETAS, FCM = another ETAS variant, LG = STEP-based, and SMA/LRWA ensembles) on the same cells, days and target events. That is a like-for-like comparison on one common sample, which is the property we need for ablations.
split_scheme: Retrospective: fit on 16 Apr 2005 to 1 Jun 2009, test on 1 Jun to 1 Sep 2009, both chronological. The parameters re-estimated on the whole catalogue did not differ significantly from the learning-set values, which serves as a stability check. Prospective: the model was frozen and submitted to the independent CSEP testing centre (ETH Zurich), which ran it daily from 1 Aug 2009 with no modeller access to the outcomes. This was a true pre-registered prospective test, assessed after 5 years (Taroni et al. 2018) and again in 2024.
metrics: Lombardi & Marzocchi 2010a: residual analysis with Ogata's transformed time (should be a unit-rate Poisson process), the KS1 test for exponential inter-event residuals, the Runs test for independence, a U(k+1) vs U(k) scatter plot, and a cumulative reliability diagram of the spatial distribution. CSEP standard tests: N-test (number), L-test and CL-test (likelihood), S-test (space), M-test (magnitude), and T/W-tests (pairwise information gain per earthquake). Brehmer et al. 2024: the Poisson log score and quadratic (Brier-type) score as proper scoring rules, Diebold-Mariano tests on score differences, and mean-reliability diagrams with consistency bands.
unit_of_metric: Pooled over all cells and days (CSEP likelihood tests). Number tests are region-wide. Brehmer et al. use mean scores over all bins, including bins with zero events, and treat per-cell score differences as diagnostics only.
baseline_strength: CSEP compares models against each other and against time-independent (smoothed-seismicity) reference models. In 2018 the 1-day ETAS models were consistent with the observed number and magnitudes, and one ETAS version was also consistent in space. Ensembles were as good as the best single model. In Brehmer et al. 2024 (Poisson score, lower is better): LRWA 2.69, LM 2.71, SMA 2.73, FCM 2.80, LG 3.02. The DM test could not separate LM (this paper's ETAS) from LRWA, SMA or FCM, but it beat LG. So the 'best' model was statistically tied with the ensembles.
calibration: Lombardi & Marzocchi 2010a used a cumulative reliability diagram of the spatial forecast (forecast cell fractions in 10 equally populated bins vs observed fractions). Its 95% error bars came from applying the same analysis to 1,000 synthetic catalogues simulated from the fitted ETAS model, conditioned on the real learning history. The bars therefore reflect clustering-induced variability, not a Poisson or binomial approximation. Observed points: 1.6e-3 -> 1.8e-3, 1.2e-2 -> 1.4e-2, 1.1e-1 -> 1.3e-1, 1.7e-1 -> 2.2e-1, all close to the diagonal. Brehmer et al. 2024: LM stays near the diagonal of the mean-reliability diagram; FCM, LG and SMA often leave the consistency bands. No recalibration was fitted.
calibration_under_drift: There was no formal calibration-in-the-large test against a validation period. The number test is a calibration-in-the-large check (total forecast vs observed count), and the papers show that it is badly misjudged when counts are treated as Poisson. Werner et al. 2010 found that 4 of the yearly counts fell outside the 95% Poisson interval (about 1 in 20 expected) and one fell beyond the 99.99% quantile. A negative binomial fitted much better. Non-stationarity (time-varying background, local alpha) is named as the main source of misfit. No recalibration method was proposed.
uncertainty_of_gain: This is the key lesson. (1) Lombardi & Marzocchi 2010b (BSSA) simulated ETAS seismicity and scored the TRUE model with the CSEP tests, which rejected it more often than the nominal rate. The reason is that ETAS forecasts vary more than Poisson allows, so independent Poisson errors per cell give intervals that are too narrow. They called for revising the testing procedures. (2) Werner et al. 2010 found the same problem for counts (overdispersion) and proposed a negative binomial number test, now implemented in floatCSEP. (3) Brehmer et al. 2024 showed that the CSEP T-test (paired information-gain comparison) uses a misspecified variance and rejected 46.5% of the time at a nominal 10% level. Its p-values are not uniform under the null. Their fix is the Diebold-Mariano test on mean score differences over all bins. They note that dependence (for example overlapping windows) needs further adjustment. Restricting to non-overlapping weekly issues did not by itself fix the miscalibrated p-values (104 and 108 of 400 p-values in the extreme tails vs 20 expected each), which points to space-time clustering as the remaining cause. (4) Lombardi & Marzocchi 2010a avoided analytic error bars and built them by simulating 1,000 catalogues from the model.
regime_coverage: The retrospective test (Jun-Sep 2009) sits entirely inside the L'Aquila aftershock regime, which is a known shift. The Italy-wide model misfit the start of that sequence. The prospective 5-year window (2009-2014) contains several sequences, including the 2012 Emilia earthquakes [uncertain]. For our project the analogy is that a single test window inside one campaign regime (summer 2026) supports conclusions only about that regime.
leakage_handling: Strong by design. (1) Prospective protocol: the model code was frozen and submitted to an independent testing centre before the outcomes existed, so neither test-period tuning nor peeking was possible. (2) Causal conditioning: each daily forecast uses only events before the window start, and in-window triggering is simulated rather than observed. (3) Retrospective test: chronological split with the parameters fixed from the learning set, while the history used for conditioning still includes the learning period. This is valid because past events are known at forecast time. (4) A known catalogue artefact (the 2005 network change) was handled by truncating the series, not by mixing regimes. Missed or acknowledged: Mc is optimistic in some zones, and the short-term incompleteness after large shocks is not modelled. For us, the CSEP 'frozen code, scored by someone else' protocol is the gold-standard version of our 'score the final test ONCE at the end of M4' rule.
test_window_hygiene: Best possible: pre-registered forecasts generated automatically by the testing centre and evaluated after fixed periods (5 years, then a 2024 re-analysis). The retrospective Jun-Sep 2009 test was one hold-out examined once before submission [uncertain: the paper does not state how many model variants were tried].
headline_results: Retrospective (Lombardi & Marzocchi 2010a): learning residuals passed KS1 (p = 0.8) but failed the Runs test (p = 0.007) because of L'Aquila; they passed it without L'Aquila (p = 0.07). Testing residuals: KS1 p = 0.14 and Runs p = 0.81, so neither test rejected. The spatial reliability diagram lay on the diagonal and inside the simulated 95% bands. Prospective (Taroni et al. 2018): the 1-day ETAS forecasts were consistent with the observed numbers and magnitudes, and one ETAS version was also consistent in space. Ensembles matched the best single model. None of the time-independent 3-month models were consistent. Brehmer et al. 2024 (Poisson score): LRWA 2.69, LM 2.71, SMA 2.73, FCM 2.80, LG 3.02. LM was best under the quadratic score. DM could not separate LM from LRWA, SMA or FCM, but showed that the clustering models beat the STEP-based LG. Methodological headline (2010b, 2024): the standard CSEP tests reject correct models too often, because Poisson-based and T-test variances ignore clustering and overdispersion. The error bars are too narrow.
code_available: Not for the 2010 ETAS code (INGV internal). The CSEP testing tools are open source: pyCSEP (https://github.com/SCECcode/pycsep, BSD-3) and floatCSEP (https://floatcsep.readthedocs.io), which includes a negative binomial N-test. Brehmer et al. 2024 code: see the paper's data/resources section [uncertain]. INGV catalogue: public (http://iside.rm.ingv.it).
takeaways_for_project:
1) Our D-013 bootstrap CI must resample whole time blocks across ALL 24 oblasts together. Alert onsets are a self-exciting space-time process: one mass drone or missile attack starts alerts in many oblasts within the same hour or two. Treating the 24 x ~1,000 test oblast-hours as independent rows (a Poisson/binomial or naive t-test CI on the Brier difference) repeats the CSEP error, with intervals that are too narrow and a true null rejected too often. The effective sample size is closer to the number of attack waves, or of test days or weeks, than to the number of rows. Resample by week (6 test weeks is very few: report the CI as wide and indicative) or by day with a moving-block bootstrap. Keep all oblasts of a block together.
2) For the primary metric (D-021, BSS vs rolling recent-rate), compare model and baseline with a Diebold-Mariano-style test on the per-hour score differences d_t = mean over oblasts of (Brier_model - Brier_recent), aggregated to one value per hour or day. Use a HAC (Newey-West) variance or a block bootstrap, never the iid variance (Brehmer et al. 2024: the iid-variance T-test rejected 46.5% at a nominal 10%). Include all scored rows, as Brehmer et al. include zero-event bins, not only hours with onsets.
3) Reliability plot (D-006): copy the Lombardi & Marzocchi idea of consistency bands. Draw the band by resampling (block bootstrap of test weeks, or Gneiting-Resin consistency bands), not by binomial sqrt(p(1-p)/n) per bin. Binomial bars per bin assume independent rows and will look falsely tight.
4) Calibration-in-the-large under drift (D-015 (c), D-021): the N-test analogue is mean predicted vs observed onset rate. Judge the size of the gap against a clustering-aware spread (for example week-to-week variability of the rolling recent-rate within the training period), not against a Poisson interval. Werner et al. found 4 of their yearly counts outside 95% Poisson limits, where about 1 in 20 is expected.
5) Rolling recent-rate as the bar to beat (D-021) is the right choice. In seismology the strong baseline for short-term forecasting is a clustering model, and a smoothed time-independent rate is the weak one. Our recent-rate baseline plays the role of a crude 'clustering-aware' reference, and climatology plays the time-independent role. Beating climatology alone proves little.
6) Features: ETAS shows that the triggering effect of the most recent events decays as a power law, (t - ti + c)^(-p). This supports keeping minutes_since_last_start, onsets_last_24h/7d and the neighbour/national-active counts, and suggests that a log transform of 'minutes since' or several decay windows may beat a single linear feature. A Hawkes-style baseline is a possible future extension but needs the human's approval (scope rule).
7) Regime boundaries: INGV cut the series at the April 2005 network change. This matches our D-007/D-015 rule never to mix the official file and alerts.in.ua in one training set or metric, and the D-020 causal standing-alert cap.
8) Pooled-model misfit: the Italy-wide ETAS failed on the start of the L'Aquila sequence because the local alpha differed. Report per-group and per-oblast results (frontline, rear, Kyiv City) and per-oblast reliability (D-013), because a pooled reliability curve can hide a badly miscalibrated unit.
9) Test hygiene: CSEP's frozen, independently scored, prospective protocol is the ideal that our 'score the final test ONCE at end of M4' rule approximates. The new-regime API check (D-015) is the only truly prospective part of our evaluation and should be described that way.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) Pre-register and freeze the model before scoring. Score once, ideally by automated code that is not edited afterwards. (b) Causal conditioning: forecasts use only history before the window start. (c) Get uncertainty bands by simulating or resampling under the actual dependence structure (synthetic catalogues or a block bootstrap), not from Poisson or binomial formulas. (d) Compare forecasts with proper scoring rules (log or Brier score) averaged over ALL scored rows, and test differences with Diebold-Mariano using HAC or block variance. (e) Use a negative binomial or other overdispersed reference when checking total counts (calibration-in-the-large). (f) Use reliability diagrams with consistency bands. (g) Start the training series at known regime or recording changes instead of mixing regimes. (h) Treat per-unit score differences as descriptive diagnostics, not formal tests, because spatial dependence and multiple testing make per-unit inference unreliable. AVOID: (1) Treating every unit-hour as an independent trial when computing CIs or p-values, which repeats the CSEP Poisson mistake. (2) The paired t-test on information gain or score difference with iid variance, which is the CSEP T-test flaw. (3) Normalising by the number of observed events (information gain per earthquake), which is undefined or unstable when there are no events, as in quiet blocks of rear oblasts. (4) Declaring a model 'rejected' or 'significantly better' from a test whose null distribution ignores clustering. (5) Generalising a pooled fit to units with different local dynamics without per-unit checks.
